cim: AI: From Artificial Intelligence to Automated Impact – aviation enters the age of the agent
cim_eredeti: AI: From Artificial Intelligence to Automated Impact – aviation enters the age of the agent
szoveg_eredeti:
AI is rapidly moving beyond the era of experimentation. For aviation and travel, the question is no longer whether artificial intelligence can produce impressive answers, generate content or analyse vast quantities of data. The more important question is what happens when AI starts to act - influencing decisions, automating processes, personalising offers, anticipating customer needs and increasingly executing tasks on behalf of travellers and businesses.

The headlines may be on the practical deployment of AI: from airline retailing, distribution and revenue management to customer service, disruption management, operations and the emerging world of agentic commerce. But this analysis questions where the technology is genuinely delivering value, where the industry is still navigating hype and experimentation, and what changes when the customer interacting with an airline may itself be an AI agent rather than a human.

That question is already becoming commercially relevant as technology providers explore AI agents that can discover, compare, book and service travel, potentially reshaping the relationship between airlines, intermediaries and customers.

The underlying argument is that AI's significance for aviation will ultimately be measured less by its intelligence than by its impact. The competitive advantage will increasingly belong not to organisations that simply possess AI capabilities, but to those capable of embedding them into the commercial and operational fabric of the business - turning better data and better predictions into faster decisions, lower friction, new revenues and more responsive customer experiences.

Drawing on discussions at T2RLEngage in London in Sep-2026, this analysis examines the transition from artificial intelligence to automated impact. It explores the emerging role of agentic AI in travel discovery and booking, the implications for airline distribution and customer ownership, and the opportunities to improve retailing, revenue management, testing and operational efficiency. It also considers the obstacles: legacy technology, fragmented data, complex integration, governance and the difficulty of validating decisions in an industry where errors can have consequences well beyond a digital transaction.

It is no longer about whether AI can demonstrate impressive capabilities. It is whether airlines can translate those capabilities into reliable, measurable business value. Competitive advantage will depend less on who adopts AI first than on who can connect it to real decisions and workflows - while retaining control of the customer relationship, the underlying data and the authority to act.

Two years ago, artificial intelligence occupied a very different place in the airline technology conversation. Today, the focus is shifting rapidly from what AI can say to what it can do.

Richard Clarke, CEO of T2RL, captured the change succinctly at the 2026 edition of T2RLEngage. The "AI story has shifted". "AI was almost nowhere two years ago," he observed, but the focus on executing transactions has now become massive, with progress moving at an incredible pace.

That is more than a technological observation. It signals a change in how aviation should think about AI's commercial significance.

The first wave of adoption has been dominated by experimentation: generating text, summarising information, assisting employees and making large volumes of data easier to interpret. These applications can be useful, but they do not necessarily change how an airline operates or competes. They can improve an existing process without fundamentally altering it.

The next stage is more consequential. AI is increasingly being developed to interpret an objective, determine the steps required to achieve it, interact with different systems and execute a task. This is the territory of agentic AI: technology that moves beyond responding to instructions towards managing workflows and taking actions within defined parameters.

This is a huge step. An AI assistant that explains a passenger's options during a disruption is useful. An AI agent that identifies suitable alternatives, checks eligibility, changes the booking and communicates the outcome could remove much of the friction from the process.

The same distinction applies commercially. Analysing customer behaviour is one capability; using that insight to assemble an offer, evaluate its value and complete a transaction is another.

Neither transition will happen uniformly across aviation. Some applications are already moving towards practical deployment, while others remain constrained by legacy systems, fragmented data and questions about reliability. But the direction is becoming clearer: the value of AI will increasingly be measured by what it enables an organisation to accomplish, rather than the sophistication of the technology itself.

The terminology surrounding AI can obscure important differences between applications. Traditional AI has long supported analytical tasks such as forecasting, classification and optimisation. Generative AI adds the ability to create content, interpret natural language and make technology more accessible through conversational interfaces. Agentic AI takes the next step by connecting reasoning to action, potentially coordinating several tasks across multiple systems to achieve an objective.

These categories overlap. An airline does not need to replace its existing technology with a single autonomous system to benefit from the progression. It can combine predictive models, generative interfaces and automated workflows, introducing greater autonomy where the business case and risk controls justify it. The practical opportunity is to move from isolated assistance towards end-to-end execution.

An airline employee might currently use several applications to investigate a problem, interpret the available information, identify an appropriate response and initiate a transaction. An AI-enabled workflow could bring these steps together, presenting the employee with a recommended action or completing routine tasks automatically within agreed boundaries.

The same principle applies to customer service, revenue management, software testing and disruption recovery. In each case, the potential benefit comes not simply from a more intelligent system, but from reducing the time, effort and friction between identifying a need and resolving it.

Yet automation should not be confused with autonomy without limits. Aviation is a complex, interconnected industry in which a seemingly straightforward decision can affect passengers, aircraft, crew, airport operations, commercial commitments and regulatory obligations. The strategic objective is therefore not to remove human involvement indiscriminately. It is to determine where decisions can safely be automated, where human approval remains necessary and how the system should respond when circumstances fall outside its operating parameters.

This will separate practical deployments from demonstrations that look impressive but struggle in the real world.

Perhaps the most consequential development discussed at T2RLEngage concerns the emergence of AI agents as intermediaries between travellers and airlines.

Surain Adyanthaya of PROS highlighted a fundamental change: AI agents are increasingly becoming the shopper, yet many airline offer platforms were not designed to be read and acted upon by machines.

The traditional customer journey is familiar: search, compare, choose and buy. The traveller visits websites, assesses alternatives and makes the decision. An agent-led journey could look very different. A traveller states an intention - perhaps a trip with specific arrival times, baggage requirements, loyalty benefits, flexibility and budget constraints. An AI agent then evaluates alternatives, weighs the trade-offs and recommends an itinerary, potentially completing the booking as well.
